title: Pros and Con(men) Why Restorative Conversations Are a Reactive Approach to Managing Behaviour
author: Mutually Assured Instruction
summary: This article critiques restorative practice programs -- particularly Real Schools, Australia's largest such provider -- arguing that restorative conversations are fundamentally reactive, targeting behaviour after it occurs rather than preventing it. The author's central contention is that a developmentally honest understanding of adolescent neurology (pre-frontal cortex immaturity until mid-twenties) makes post-hoc reflection an inherently weak behaviour management lever: teenagers need firm, supportive structures applied consistently, not reflective conversations after violations have already occurred. The piece scrutinises Real Schools' data claims, noting that pre/post survey improvements in 'school climate' and 'effective classroom behaviour' are self-reported and collected by the very teachers implementing the program -- a textbook observer-expectation confound. The author draws a distinction between proactive behaviour management systems that prevent misbehaviour through clear expectations and routines, and reactive systems that respond to it, arguing that well-designed proactive systems make expensive consultant-dependent reactive programs largely unnecessary. The article acknowledges that restorative conversations have legitimate uses for maintaining long-term relationships, but insists that for teenagers in school settings, structure, predictability, and early prevention are the load-bearing elements of behaviour management.
points: Restorative conversations ask teenagers to reflect on the causes and effects of their behaviour, but the underdeveloped pre-frontal cortex -- which will not mature until the mid-twenties -- means adolescents predictably lack the regulatory capacity this approach assumes.

Real Schools' key data metrics (school climate, effective classroom behaviour, suspension rates) are measured by the same teachers implementing the program, creating an observer-expectation confound that makes positive results unreliable without independent verification.

The distinction between proactive and reactive behaviour management is central to the critique: proactive approaches prevent misbehaviour through structure and relationship; reactive approaches like restorative conversations respond after the damage has occurred.

The author's most pointed critique is economic: restorative practice consultants benefit precisely from schools that become dependent on their ongoing services, whereas genuinely proactive behaviour systems remove the need for that ongoing dependency.

Social psychology's evidence base -- drawn from surveys, observations, and self-report rather than experimental lab settings -- is structurally harder to interpret without the confounds that inflate positive outcomes, and schools should approach vendor-produced evidence with corresponding scepticism.
quotes: We're talking about teenagers here! Teenagers with undeveloped frontal lobes, specifically their pre-frontal cortexes which will not mature until their mid-twenties and will therefore without firm and supportive boundaries to their behaviour and decision making are likely to make bad choices.
The big issue with proactive approaches is that if they're done well, you're unlikely to need a consultant long term to fix all of your problems because the problems will be minimal and actionable.

On their website Real Schools boasts a number of data points about pre and post survey feelings about student and staff in the program. My challenge here is that on their website they do not explicitly go into how the data was collected, how it was measured, what each of the categories mean. It's just a series of vagaries left to the interpretation of the reader.

If we were to conduct a study in a school which was to see if a teacher wearing a hat decreased incidences of adverse student behaviour and we communicated to staff that we were going to be measuring that over a 2 week period it would lead to a conundrum occurring. The teachers involved in the experiment are also the ones logging the data to determine the success of the experiment.
Sometimes a teacher in a hat, is just a teacher in a hat.
Not all evidence is equal. It's hard to trust a program which does not share the data which it is based upon.
